title: Denver (Adams County) well depth and costs
meta_description: Median well depth 29 ft and median yield 33 gpm near Denver in Adams County. What that means for drilling costs, water levels, and risks.
h1: Water wells around Denver in Adams County
intro_html:
In the plains around Denver in Adams County, most permitted wells are shallow and productive, but you’re also in an urbanized, heavily monitored groundwater area. Records for 8,970 permits within about 5 miles give a good picture of how deep wells run, how much water they make, and what a new well is likely to cost.

If you’re looking at land or a home around places like Glendale, Derby, Welby, or North Washington, use the nearby well data as your reality check before you commit to a lot or a driller.

sections.heading: How deep wells run here and why
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Denver in Adams County, wells are generally shallow. The median total depth is 29 feet, and the middle half run 20–45 feet. About 94% of wells are under 100 feet, and only 2% go deeper than 300 feet, with the deepest on record at 2,023 feet.

Most permits list an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with some specifically calling out Alluvial or Denver aquifers, but administratively these are all treated as Denver Basin aquifer wells. Around the river valleys and low spots, shallow alluvial sands and gravels help keep depths down. A driller here usually bids assuming a short hole, but they still have to be ready in case a specific site needs to chase water much deeper than the neighborhood norm.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Where yields are reported near Denver, they’re generally strong. The median reported pump yield is 33.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 15.0 and 73.8 gpm. About 75% of wells with data make 15 gpm or more, 21% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and only 4% sit between 1–5 gpm. None in the records report under 1 gpm.

For a household exempt well, Colorado’s practical pumping limit is 15 gpm, so most of these wells are capable of delivering more than you’re legally allowed to run. Irrigation and commercial uses still need to match their water-rights and augmentation plans, but from a physical capacity standpoint, the Denver-area plains are not a low-yield hotspot based on these records.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they’re doing over time
sections.html:
Static water levels around Denver in Adams County are quite shallow. The median depth to water is 10 feet below ground surface, with the middle half between 7 and 17 feet. That’s why so many wells don’t have to be drilled very deep to find water.

Looking at the trend, median measured water levels were about 26 feet in the 1960s, then around 9 feet in the 2000s, 11 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet again in the 2020s. That suggests water levels rose compared with the 1960s and have stayed relatively stable over the last few decades. Even so, local conditions can vary block to block, so don’t assume your lot looks exactly like the decade averages.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Drilling and monitoring around Denver has been steady for a long time. Permits start showing up in the 1950s with 216 records, then 169 in the 1960s and 104 in the 1970s. Activity jumps in the 1980s with 440 permits, 2,034 in the 1990s, 1,231 in the 2000s, 2,060 in the 2010s, and 737 already in the 2020s. The newest permits are from 2025.

This is a heavily monitored groundwater area: about 69% of permits are monitoring wells, with domestic/household uses at 12% and irrigation at 2%. The most active drillers in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 3,204 wells, Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) with 270, and Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.) with 141. When you see those names on nearby permits, you’re looking at contractors who know the local formations well.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
Ground here is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and the typical drilling rate runs about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 29 feet, the drilled hole itself pencils out around $1,400–$2,000. That’s just the borehole.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well around this depth generally falls in the $7,400–$14,000 range. Because so many wells in this area are shallow, most bids will assume a short hole with a contingency if you have to chase water deeper. The big cost risks here are less about extreme depth and more about site access, utilities, and any special construction requirements tied to contamination concerns.

sections.heading: Risks to check: contamination, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
The records don’t show a lot of low-yield wells here, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gpm, so the bigger concern in this urban corridor is water quality, not quantity. Within about 10 miles there are 662 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 182 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, with no historic mine features noted.

Before buying, budget for a full water test panel that includes PFAS, plus the usual bacteria, nitrates, and metals. With such shallow median water levels (around 10 feet), proper well construction and sealing, and sound septic design, are critical to keep surface contaminants out. Check required setbacks from septic systems and building foundations early; shallow groundwater can also influence basement and foundation drainage design.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot near Denver
sections.html:
If you’re eyeing land around Glendale, Four Square Mile, Derby, or Welby, pull the well logs within a mile or so and look at three things: total depth, yield, and static water level. Around Denver in Adams County, the typical well depth is only 29 feet, with strong median yield at 33.0 gpm and a median water level about 10 feet down, so most lots don’t face deep-drilling risk.

What you do need is a clear plan for water rights, well permitting through the Colorado Division of Water Resources, and water-quality testing given the number of nearby monitoring and cleanup sites. Get your well, septic, and house layout coordinated at the design stage so you meet setbacks and avoid surprises later.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Denver in Adams County?
faq.a: Well records within about 5 miles of Denver in Adams County show a median total depth of 29 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 45 feet. About 94% of wells are under 100 feet. A small minority run much deeper, up to 2,023 feet, so it’s smart to review nearby logs for your specific block before assuming your well will be shallow.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Denver usually produce?
faq.a: Reported yields here are generally strong. The median yield is 33.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 15.0 and 73.8 gpm. About 75% of wells with data produce 15 gpm or more, 21% are 5–15 gpm, and only 4% fall between 1–5 gpm. None in the dataset report under 1 gpm, which is encouraging for household use.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near Denver, Colorado?
faq.a: In the Denver-area plains of Adams County, drilling through Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock typically runs $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 29 feet, the borehole alone is roughly $1,400–$2,000. A complete domestic well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $7,400–$14,000, depending on site access and specific installation needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink around Denver in Adams County?
faq.a: The data show many monitoring wells and a lot of environmental activity: 662 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 182 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That doesn’t mean every well is unsafe, but it does mean you should test thoroughly. Include PFAS, bacteria, nitrates, and metals in your lab panel and repeat testing periodically, especially for shallow wells.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping near Denver in Adams County?
faq.a: Median static water levels in this area were about 26 feet below ground surface in the 1960s, then around 9 feet in the 2000s, 11 feet in the 2010s, and 9 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water levels rose compared with the 1960s and have stayed relatively stable in recent decades. Still, conditions can vary locally, so check recent measurements on nearby wells.
